title: SYSK Gets Weird Playlist: The Max Headroom Incident
summary: Rerun playlist episode "SYSK Gets Weird Playlist: The Max Headroom Incident." Josh and Chuck explain the Max Headroom character (from the 1984 film and 1985-86 TV series, played by Matt Frewer) and then recount the unsolved November 22, 1987 Chicago broadcast intrusion, in which a man in a Max Headroom mask hijacked WGN's signal during a Bears sportscast and later WTTW's PBS broadcast of Doctor Who. They cover the FCC and FBI investigation, the theory that the intrusion needed only modest equipment, the BBS-era suspects (Eric Furnier and Shea St. John, and Bowie Pogue's account of two men in Chicago), and the case remaining unsolved. The episode ends with listener mail about Dwayne Allman's "eat a peach" quote.
topics: Doctor Who Horror of Fang Rock

entities.name: Doctor Who: The Horror of Fang Rock

segments.title: Cold open and welcome
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode about a 1987 Chicago incident in which a man in a Max Headroom mask took over a TV station, and the show is welcomed.

segments.title: Motherboard article as source
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh credit Alex Pasternak's Motherboard article on the Max Headroom hack as the main source and mention the hosts' past blogging for the site.

segments.title: Max Headroom movie and show background
segments.summary: The 1984 film and the TV series are described, including Matt Frewer playing the character, the Edison Carter origin, the origin of the name from a parking garage sign, and the Max Headroom New Coke ad.

segments.title: Blipverts and the show's premise
segments.summary: The hosts describe the show's dystopian premise in which TV networks control the world and blipverts, compressed 30-second ads, are used to keep viewers from changing channels.

segments.title: Max Headroom makeup and cult following
segments.summary: The character was made with prosthetics and video effects rather than CGI, with Matt Frewer acting in makeup that took about four hours to apply. The character gained a cult following among geeks and cyberpunks.

segments.title: Geek culture and setting the scene in Chicago
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how geek and nerd culture was derided in the 1980s and set up the November 22, 1987 Chicago event, with the Bears having beaten the Lions that day.

segments.title: First intrusion during WGN sportscast
segments.summary: At 9:14 p.m., during a sportscast on WGN Channel 9 with Dan Roan reviewing a Bears game, the signal was broken into by a man in a Max Headroom mask with no audio. WGN engineers switched to a backup transmitter, and the FCC was called in.

segments.title: Second intrusion during Doctor Who on WTTW
segments.summary: About two hours later, during a PBS WTTW broadcast of Doctor Who's The Horror of Fang Rock, a second intrusion occurred lasting about a minute and 22 seconds. The hosts suggest viewers search for the footage.

segments.title: Contents of the Max Headroom broadcast
segments.summary: The hosts describe the intrusion's visuals: a masked man with corrugated metal behind him, and garbled speech attacking Chuck Swirsky of the Bulls, a new Coke can, Clutch Cargo theme humming, the WGN 'world's greatest newspaper' reference, and a man in a prairie-style dress spanking a bare rear with a fly swatter.

segments.title: Public reaction and legal consequences
segments.summary: The public reaction was mixed, with some interviewed on WGN and a Doctor Who fan who was angry about the interruption. The FCC warned of fines up to $100,000 and a year in jail, and the FBI and Chicago PD also looked into it.

segments.title: How the intrusion may have been done
segments.summary: Investigators first assumed expensive equipment and high electricity use, but FCC investigator Michael Marcus later suggested a dish-sized setup on a nearby rooftop could have overpowered the signal between the studio and towers at the John Hancock building and Sears Tower.

segments.title: Investigation dead ends and the unsolved case
segments.summary: Investigators gave up due to no injuries and limited resources. The FBI analyzed enhanced video frames, but the only visual clue was the spinning corrugated metal. The statute of limitations expired in 1993.

segments.title: BBS messages and the Chameleon post
segments.summary: Two days after the incident, a BBS user called The Chameleon described how the intrusion was done, showing the tech scene of the time. The hosts explain that few theories have held up.

segments.title: Eric Furnier and Shea St. John theory
segments.summary: A rumored suspect was musician Eric Furnier, who made the Shea St. John YouTube series and was in the band Blood Farmers in Bloomington, Indiana. Friends said he was not capable of it and the theory is considered a dead end.

segments.title: Bowie Pogue's account and the brothers theory
segments.summary: Bowie Pogue, a 13-year-old BBS user in 1987, recalled two older men in Chicago with a computer-filled apartment who hinted at a big thing on the night of November 22. Pasternak contacted them, but they did not respond.

segments.title: Unsolved status and wrap-up
segments.summary: The hosts conclude that the case remains unsolved and that it is a legend in hacker and geek culture, and recommend reading the Motherboard article.

segments.title: Listener mail: Dwayne Allman eat a peach
segments.summary: Listener Jesse Gaudette contends the Allman Brothers album Eat a Peach title came from Dwayne Allman's quip about eating a peach for peace, made after a reporter asked what he would do for the Vietnam war effort.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners, invite feedback by Twitter, Facebook, and email, and point to the website.
